title: Choose the stronger follow-up
scenario: A product announcement draft came back well structured but too long and a little salesy. You liked the opening paragraph and the three feature bullets; everything after them needs work.
task: Pick the follow-up message you would actually send.
promptB: Keep the opening paragraph and the three bullets exactly as they are. Cut everything after the bullets. Rewrite the two sentences that say 'revolutionary' so they state the change plainly.

feedback.a: 'Better' has no target — the model guesses, and you end up re-reading a new draft while hunting for the same old problems.
feedback.b: It points at the exact parts to keep, the exact parts to cut and the exact flaw to fix — three surgical edits in one short message.

hints: Which follow-up tells the model what NOT to touch?
Count the concrete instructions each message contains.
explanation: A follow-up works when it narrows the search: keep this, cut that, fix those sentences. 'Make it better' re-rolls the dice instead of steering the draft — you get a new version to review from scratch, with no guarantee the parts you liked survive.
